#1984. Crawley Town chief has his say on whether 3pm football blackout is still relevant

The Premier League and EFL are set to hold serious conversations about the blackout’s future next year with pretty much every TV slot now exhausted.

Removing the blackout – which is a rule that prevents live football matches from being broadcast on television or streaming services between 2.45pm and 5.15pm on Saturdays – could have a detrimental effect on attendances and finances, especially clubs in the lower tiers like Crawley Town.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The blackout is under threat and television rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30 and last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout – introduced in 2003 by UEFA as Article 48.

But this summer there appeared to be a shift in emphasis, with Masters saying there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged caution and suggested the health of the football pyramid should come first.

The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. No other major country qualifies for the blackout - it is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

CEO Allman gave his personal opinion – and not necessarily that of the club – about the situation and what it would mean if it ended.

He said: “My personal opinion is that the 3pm blackout currently works well in protecting the current football pyramid. I hear the arguments about it not being in place in other countries, but there is no pyramid like the UK pyramid so am not sure it is a fair comparison.

"We see notable increases in attendances during international breaks as well as drop offs for Tuesday night games for example where they are available on SkySports+ so in general, whilst removing the blackout, would arguably increase the exposure of clubs like Crawley, would levy that with actual attendances dropping off, which whilst having the obvious financial implication, will also have impacts on atmospheres and the general match-day feel.”

So it’s clear whether he would oppose the ending of the blackout? “I wouldn’t be in favour - as I say, I think the pyramid is what stands us apart from other countries and sports, and with that, would encourage fans to go out and experience the full pyramid, rather than looking for more Premier League games on TV.”

He added: “Whilst I understand the argument of increased coverage, I wouldn’t levy that against supporters being in the stadium, buying a pint, eating a burger, cheering their team on and in turn, financially supporting the club to allow us to kick on across the board.”

#1983. Kevin De Bruyne to leave Napoli 'the sooner the better', his wife announces: Man City legend, 35, desperate to quit his 'not nice existence' after rows with team-mates, bosses and fan issues

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:58 EST, 13 November 2026

Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles in Naples and desire to move back home to Belgium one day.

De Bruyne, 35, joined Napoli in the summer of 2025 after leaving Manchester City following a legendary ten-year spell.

But things haven't gone to plan in Italy, with De Bruyne struggling for fitness in his first season, while he also clashed with former boss Antonio Conte.

The situation hasn't improved much this time around under Max Allegri as Napoli currently sit 10th in Serie A, and reports broke earlier this season that the Belgian midfielder was involved in a dressing room bust-up with team-mates.

And De Bruyne's wife Michele, who he married in 2017, reflected on the turbulence in an interview with Belgian magazine NINA back in September.

'Of course, we think about the future together,' he said. 'And increasingly often, we say to each other: "We are going to live here in Limburg. The sooner we get here, the better".'

Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles living in Naples

De Bruyne moved to Napoli in the summer of 2025 after a glittering 10 years at Manchester City

Limburg is a province in Belgium, and although Michelle insisted that she thought Naples was a beautiful place to live with great weather and food, she spoke about the toll that life in Italy has had on her partner and their three children, Mason, Rome and Suri.

'Kevin leads a very restricted life in Napoli,' she added. 'It's not much fun for him. Besides, we can't do anything together as a family in the city. That's the other side of the coin, isn't it?

'In Manchester, it was different. Where we lived, people had seen us so often that it wasn’t special anymore. We could walk out the door there without a single photo being taken. In Naples, that is impossible.'

She later added: 'At a certain point, football is no longer the priority. You have achieved everything, done everything. Why would you then turn your children’s lives upside down?'

De Bruyne, who is one of the highest paid players in Italy, signed a two-year contract when he arrived at Napoli but it wasn't certain that he would make it into the second part of that deal in the summer.

Reflecting on his first year ahead of the World Cup, De Bruyne insisted he was 'happy' that Conte had departed.

'Obviously it was difficult for me because Conte has a very different vision of football to mine,' De Bruyne said.

'In truth, I never had the opportunity to play in my preferred position. In any case, I always tried to give my all for the team. We played very defensively. If you try to win every game by a one-goal margin with a 4-5-1 formation, you play a certain type of football.

De Bruyne signed a two-year deal at Napoli and is unlikely to extend his time in Italy

'At the start of the season, we sat back even deeper. Our centre-forward scored just 10 goals, so you know the statistics are not going to be great…'

He later added: 'For me, yes (I'm happy Conte has gone). As far as I am concerned, he was not obliged to stay. There were promises made last summer on the way that we would be playing, but at the end of the day not much of it happened.

'I found that a pity. Football needs to be enjoyable, and unfortunately, I found that aspect lacking.

'There’s no point beating around the bush, we have different visions of football. I never got to play in my position under Conte.'

#1982. Lewes down Town to reach Sussex Senior Cup last eight

On a damp evening on the Sussex coast, Lewes defeated Step 4 Town 2-1 to make the last eight.

Two goals of varying difficulty from Bassett laid the foundations for the win, with the Rooks then withstanding Town’s pressure after a Sonny Walsh strike to make progress.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

While it was not the most fluent outing for Lewes, several performances on an evening of experimentation will give reason for optimism.

The Rooks arrived at The Saffrons with six changes to their starting XI, including Josh Spinks’ return as captain and a debut for new attacking signing Kwesi Ntim.

Ntim, who has scored 20 goals in 33 games for Lingfield in 2026, was a bright spark early on, cutting in from the left flank and posing problems for the home defence.

Genuine chances took a while to arrive on the south coast, with the opening stages dominated by safe possession football.

After 25 minutes, however, Lewes created their first threat as Bassett worked space on the right and forced goalkeeper Chris Winterton to punch a cross into the path of Brian Garzon, whose right-footed effort was cleared off the line.

The Rooks slowly built the pressure from here, with Tyler Christian-Law and Mackenzie Richardson driving at goal before the opener soon arrived.

In the 37th minute, Ntim added a flash of brilliance with a pacey drive in from the left, setting up Richardson for a first-time effort at goal. With ex-Rooks ‘keeper Winterton spilling the ball, Bassett was on hand to tap home.

Richardson had another bite at a goal of his own before the break, but Winterton stood up well to a rising effort from the left of the box to keep the score at 0-1.

Lewes did not hesitate in doubling down on their advantage at the start of the second half, and Bassett was the man to deliver again.

Barely 30 seconds into the half, the forward stormed down the right and cut into the box before producing an audacious chip on Winterton that dropped into the top left corner.

It was a moment of magic, and whether Bassett had meant it or not, nobody could begrudge the striker his fourth goal of the season thus far.

The Rooks got into a rhythm after this, regularly wriggling free of Town's attentions and finding space on the counter without truly putting the game to bed.

Bassett and Ntim were similarly denied in the area, while Garzon had at least two notable chances while cutting inside that flew inches wide of the post.

All the while, Town were never out of the tie, and they got their spark in the 61st minute.

Sonny Walsh was set free on the right of the box and blasted an effort past Louis Rogers to halve the deficit.

Town had two brilliant chances to level the scores in the final 30 minutes, but as has been their story in the last few weeks, luck was against them.

A ball in from the right was stabbed over the crossbar from close range, and in the dying stages, Walsh was again set free on the right but blasted over the target.

Equally, Lewes could have added to their advantage as substitute Omar Al-Seadi prodded wide of the left post when excellently teed up by a combination of Bassett and Kurtis Cumberbatch.

Altogether, Lewes were relieved to hear the final whistle as they made it to the final eight, but were good value for the result across the 90 minutes.

At the time of writing, the timing of the draw for the Quarter-Finals, and the dates of this round, are yet to be announced.

We anticipate news of both in due course, and urge supporters to keep tabs on our social media pages for the latest updates.

This Saturday, the Rooks are back in Isthmian Premier Division action away at Ramsgate FC.

With Lewes in 5th and Ramsgate - with a game in hand - just three points behind in 6th, it has all the makings of an excellent game at Southwood Stadium. Kick-off is at 3pm.

Leeds United marksman Dominic Calvert-Lewin is in the wrong international era, according to former England forward Mark Hateley.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He currently sits at the chief understudy to Harry Kane, who was recently crowned winner of the coveted Ballon d’Or award.

Hateley, who won 32 England caps between 1984 and 1992 and had a loan spell at Leeds in 1996, has rued the timing of Calvert-Lewin’s emergence on the international scene.

He told The Yorkshire Post via London.Bet: “I'm going to say the only way that Calvert-Lewin will get a game is if he's (Kane) injured, because I think he will be first in. He's got to play the long game. Harry's going to play for a long time, I think.

“Sports science and everything going forward is all geared for playing longer. The way Harry lives his life, his lifestyle, his ability to adapt as a player... Calvert-Lewin is in the wrong place at the wrong time, wrong era.

“He's just got himself stuck behind an absolute legend of a player that just seems to get better and better and better. He'll (Kane) crush 150 plus games, the goal tally will go up and up and up. That's who you've just got to sit behind, but you've got to be ready.”

Calvert-Lewin may not be England’s number nine but he is certainly the chief marksman at Elland Road. He has enjoyed a career rejuvenation in West Yorkshire, notching 20 goals across 51 appearances since his free transfer move from Everton in the summer of 2025.

Hateley said: “You've got to be doing your stuff at Leeds, you've got to be scoring goals at Leeds, staying fit, playing well.

“I think the problem with Calvert-Lewin is, in his younger career, there was a lot of niggly injuries. A lot of setbacks, holding him back, not being able to get on runs.

“When you're being selected for an international set-up, you have to be consistently on top of your game. You're persistently good. You're always there knocking at the door. That's what Calvert-Lewin's got to do now.

“He's got to keep himself fit. He's got to do good things with Leeds and score goals. It's as simple as that.”

#1969. 'A significant shift was necessary' - Crawley Town owners break silence with open letter to fans

Reds supporters have been calling out for communication from Raphael Khalili and co following the poor start to the season, the sacking of Colin Kazim-Richards and the embarrassing FA Cup exit to Wimborne Town.

But following the club confirming Kevin Blackwell’s appointment as head coach until the end of the season, the ownership group published an open letter to fans.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

In the letter they ‘take full responsibility for the direction of this football club’ and recognised ‘significant shift in direction was necessary’ and that ‘difficult decisions have now been made’.

They also gave updates on strengthening the club’s leadership and the the ownership group.

From the Ownership Group and Board of Directors of Crawley Town Football Club

First and foremost, we want to thank every Crawley Town supporter for their continued patience, loyalty and commitment to this Football Club during what has undoubtedly been a difficult period.

We recognise that our start to the season has fallen well below the standards we expect, and more importantly, the standards that you, our supporters, deserve. We understand the frustration, the disappointment and the questions being asked. We also recognise that our communication in recent weeks has not been what it should be.

Over the past month, we have been working tirelessly behind the scenes to assess every aspect of the club and put in place the new structures and processes required to take us forward into a positive new chapter.

As owners, we take full responsibility for the direction of this football club. We have never underestimated the privilege of being entrusted with Crawley Town, nor the responsibilities and expectations that come with it.

It became clear that a significant shift in direction was necessary. Some difficult decisions have now been made, but we firmly believe they are the best decisions for protecting the long-term interests of Crawley Town Football Club.

Today, we want to share with you some of the changes that we are making in order to demonstrate our commitment to changing the direction of the Club for the better.

First Team Management: Following the recent changes to our football management structure, we undertook an extensive search to identify the right person to lead Crawley Town going forward.

Over the past several weeks, we have spoken with and interviewed numerous experienced and highly regarded managers. Throughout this process, our priority has always been to make the right appointment for the Club, rather than rushing into a decision.

At the same time, we have been extremely encouraged by the impact Kevin Blackwell has made since taking charge. His experience, leadership and understanding of the challenges we face have been evident, and we have seen a marked improvement in the players' performances, engagement and attitude.

With the team remaining unbeaten in the league under Kevin's leadership, there have already been encouraging signs of greater stability, resilience and togetherness within the squad.

Having carefully considered all of our options and building upon the positive impact that we have already seen from Kevin, we firmly believe that he is the right man to lead Crawley Town for the remainder of the season, and we are pleased to confirm his appointment as First Team Manager.

Kevin has our full confidence and support, and we will be further strengthening his coaching team with the addition of another assistant coach in due course.

Our immediate focus is now on giving Kevin, his staff and the players every opportunity to succeed, restoring confidence and building the consistency required to climb the league table.

Strengthening the Club's Leadership: We are currently in the process of strengthening our senior executive structure to provide greater expertise and support across both our football and off-field operations.

We expect to provide further details subject to the necessary approvals from the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) and the EFL.

We believe that establishing a strong, experienced and accountable executive structure is fundamental to building a successful and sustainable football club.

Strengthening Our Ownership Group: We are delighted to announce and welcome Jonathan Meller to our Ownership Group. Jonathan brings extensive experience and knowledge from more than a decade of involvement in football and has a long-standing relationship with members of our Ownership Group. He has experience in helping clubs progress and sees Crawley Town as the perfect opportunity to help a club grow and move up the leagues.

We believe Jonathan's insight, relationships and understanding of the industry will be another valuable addition as we continue to develop the Club.

Recruitment, Data and Football Operations: Our review has also identified the need to modernise and strengthen the way the Club operates, particularly in the areas of player recruitment, performance analysis and internal processes. We will be able to announce the appointment of a new Head of Recruitment in the days/coming weeks, who will play an important role in contributing to our future football strategy. In parallel, we are developing a comprehensive new data-led and eyes-on recruitment strategy, alongside improved systems and processes throughout the Club.

Our ambition is to build a more intelligent, efficient and structured football operation, where recruitment decisions are supported by robust analysis, clear football principles and a long-term vision and culture.

These changes will not happen overnight, but they are essential if we are to establish the foundations for lasting success.

Commercial Growth and New Opportunities: Off the pitch, we are equally focused on developing the Club's commercial potential and creating opportunities that extend beyond the traditional boundaries of a League Two football club. We are in the final stages of an exciting new commercial partnership, which we expect to announce shortly.

We believe this relationship has the potential to introduce Crawley Town to a significantly wider, global audience, creating new opportunities for the Club, our partners and our supporters.

Our ambition remains to build a club that is competitive on the pitch, commercially progressive off it and firmly connected to its community.

We appreciate that announcements, words and promises ultimately mean very little without results on the pitch.

We will be judged by our actions, and rightly so: We are not asking anyone to ignore the difficulties of recent months or pretend that everything has been good enough. It hasn't. But we do ask that we now look forward together rather than backwards and divided.

Football is never a straight line. Every club experiences difficult periods, setbacks and moments when its character is tested. It is during these moments, more than any other, that the strength of a football club's community becomes so important.

The supporters are, and always will be, the heartbeat of Crawley Town. Your loyalty, your passion and your support are what give this Club its identity and purpose.

We understand that support must be earned through performances and results, and we accept our responsibility to deliver both. However, we also believe that the strongest football clubs are those that stand together through the difficult moments, not just the successful ones.

Our upcoming fixture against Fleetwood is an important moment for this football club. We want to use it as an opportunity to draw a line under the difficult start to our season and begin a new chapter, together. Fill the stands, make your voices heard and get behind Kevin and the players from the very first whistle.

We know the difference a united crowd can make, particularly when a team needs confidence and belief.

Let Fleetwood be the moment we come together, turn the page and start building the momentum that will define the rest of our season: There is still a long way to go, plenty of football to be played and everything to fight for. We have absolute belief in our ability to turn our fortunes around.

We remain as committed and determined today as we were on the day we took ownership of this Football Club. Our ambition has not changed, and neither has our belief in what Crawley Town can become. There will undoubtedly be further challenges along the way, but we are determined to face them with honesty, resilience and a shared sense of purpose.

To every supporter who has continued to turn up, travel, sing and stand by the team during this difficult period, thank you. Your commitment does not go unnoticed or unappreciated.

For and on behalf of the Ownership Group & Board of Directors Crawley Town Football Club​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

#1968. Messi was a deity among Argentina’s unholy rabble

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

#1967. Arsenal star Max Dowman smashes Jude Bellingham's record - but a less-familiar name should catch Thomas Tuchel's eye ahead of Euro 2028: THINGS WE LEARNED from England U21's defeat to Portugal

Published: 16:46 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EST, 13 November 2026

Max Dowman smashed Jude Bellingham's record on an icy cold night in Bristol to become the youngest player to ever play for England's Under-21s.

The 16-year-old was sent on with 30 minutes to go by Lee Carsley in a move that energised an Ashton Gate crowd that went home frustrated after a 1-0 defeat inflicted by Afonso Moreira's first half goal.

But this was to be Dowman's night, smashing the previous record set by Bellingham when he made his England Under-21 debut against Kosovo in 2020 aged 17 years, two months and six days old. Dowman does not turn 17 until December 31.

Under-21s boss Lee Carsley has been keen long before this international break to try to shield Dowman from the weight of expectation.

But on he came, replacing the lively Amario Cozier-Duberry with a smile on his face and a quiet confidence that he didn't take long to show off, bursting past two Portuguese markers before four huddled together to gang up on him.

Breaking records is nothing new to a player that already holds one for being the Premier League's youngest-ever goalscorer, thanks to his goal against Everton last season.

Max Dowman wrote his name into the record books once more, playing for England Under-21s

Dowman came on to rich applause on a cold night in Bristol to shatter Jude Bellingham's record

The Arsenal teenager was lively playing off the right as he now targets the 2027 U21 Euros

Dowman is both the youngest player to ever win the Premier League and his outing in the Champions League against Slavia Prague last season saw the then-15-year-old become the youngest-ever player to appear in that competition.

By the time next summer's European Championships, which England will attempt to win for a third successive time, rolls around, rising star Dowman could well have earned the right to be this team's main man.

'We've only got three games left before the Euros [next summer],' Carsley explained.

'So it's important that he puts himself in the shop window to be on the plane.

'It's important that he keeps playing well, getting minutes, showing a really good attitude, like he has done.

'I thought he was outstanding when he came on tonight. I thought all of the subs made a real impact.

'I thought Max was unlucky not to get an assist... he made a great pass to Mikey Moore.

'He took up some really good positions, both in the 10 and out wide, he's got a big future ahead.'

His immense talent was one reason why Arsenal sent Ethan Nwaneri, who Dowman played alongside for part of his cameo, to Marseille on loan, and then similarly to Borussia Dortmund, eager not to block the 16-year-old's pathway.

Carsley knows the diamond he has on his hands and will want to take great care in helping polish a player that this crowd, this England team and this management group know has genuine world class potential.

Speaking of Nwaneri, this felt like a big camp for him. A big camp in the sense that he's falling down the pecking order at Dortmund and is back with a manager that has been so vital in his development.

Nwaneri was part of that 2025 group that won the Euros in front of Thomas Tuchel and he'll have seen the likes of Elliot Anderson and Alex Scott kick on to get to the seniors.

As previously mentioned, Nwaneri was moved out of the way by Arsenal to aid Dowman's development, not an easy pill for a player as talented as he is to stomach when his own development journey is at such a critical juncture given he is, to the surprise of many, still only 19.

'I think we have to remember his age as well,' Carsley added when asked about Nwaneri by Daily Mail Sport.

'He's very young is Ethan and he's another one that we've got a lot of hope for. He's got a lot of potential.'

Ethan Nwaneri was pushed to the side at Arsenal to benefit Dowman but England is different

Lee Carsley has been a crucial figure in the development of Nwaneri and this camp was timely

It was telling that even when Dowman came on, even with the groundswell of excitement at his introduction, it was Carsley's call to keep Nwaneri in his preferred No 10 position with Dowman slotting in on the right.

Nwaneri has only started four games on loan at Dortmund this season and has not managed a single start in the Champions League.

His close control, his quick burst over five yards and the fluidity of his movement was a timely reminder that yes, Dowman is the rising star everyone came out to see, but Nwaneri won't get pushed to the side again without a fight.

Amario Cozier-Duberry is a name not all will be familiar with but come next summer, with the Euros in his sights and promotion to the Premier League on the agenda with Middlesbrough, that could all be about to change.

The 21-year-old has had to be very patient, waiting until last month to make his debut at this level after years of finding himself overlooked.

Here, in what was just his third Under-21 appearance, he showed over the course of 61 minutes why the days of being looked past should be over.

One of the big frustrations in the FA right now at Under-21 level is the lack of touchline wingers. Rio Ngumoha, still only 18, has never been capped at the level and has instead been catapulted into the first team, while many, like Ethan Nwaneri, prefer playing inside.

'The more we can get our wide players one v one the better,' Carsley said. 'I think sometimes we leave them isolated and the opposition are able to double up on them.

Amario Cozier-Duberry is not a household name at international level but his talent is immense

'It's important that our game plan can't just be to get the ball wide and hope for the best.'

Dowman, on in place of Cozier-Duberry is a 10, rather than a right winger which is where he came on, and so a player like Cozier-Duberry, who is on loan at Middlesbrough from Brighton & Hove Albion, is worth his weight in gold.

Here in Bristol he was routinely drawing two defenders and at times three; Portugal knew full well how a quick flip-flap of the ball, or one clipped pass over the top, was enough for the Englishman to take the top off the back-line.

His loan at Bolton Wanderers last season complicated an international journey that has seen him play at Under-16, Under-17, Under-18, Under-19 and Under-20 level, but that's all in the past.

England need a genuine, pacy threat out wide if they are to win a third straight Euros. Cozier-Duberry showed here exactly why he should be it.

“With AC Milan as our cornerstone, which will always be the driving force behind all our initiatives, we intend to build a world-class sports and entertainment platform capable of shaping the future of Milan and European sports, and bringing it back to the forefront of the global stage.”

However, what has his career looked like so far and how can he help the Rossoneri take the next level?

In terms of his own reputation, he started his career working in selling TV time before moving to be a senior accountant at Palace Sports and Entertainment, sound familiar? From there, he got his first major move, becoming a director of marketing at NASCAR, where he stayed from 1998 to 2005.

After his early experience in basketball, he then moved away from the track and back onto the court where he joined the Brooklyn Jets as their new CEO. Tasked with transforming the club into a more modern brand, he franchised the club – taking them from Brooklyn to New Jersey – and brought several sports and events to the Barclays Center, which opened in 2012, as Sportico reported.

From there, he then headed to Roc Nation, taking a role as their ‘President & Chief of Branding and Strategy’. From artists to athletes, Yormark worked with some of the biggest names and brands in the world from 2019 to 2022 and was a major part of the brand earning the rights for the Super Bowl halftime shows.

It’s worth noting that he’s also worked with Milan in this period, as they partnered in 2020. On a side note, it’ll be interesting to see if these links help any further with the ongoing speculation about the Diavolo and Endrick, who is also represented by the brand.

To join the Milan Sports and Entertainment company, he leaves behind a role with Big 12, where he had held a role since the summer of 2022. Within his first few months as its commissioner, he secured media rights deals with ESPN and Fox to help stabilise the league.

The Kansas City Star continues, stating that he also oversaw expansions into ‘Arizona, Arizona State, Colorado and Utah’, as well as keeping men’s and women’s basketball in Kansas City.

Given that he’ll be working heavily with the hope of making a Milan NBA team, this is relevant experience. Importantly, too, he has already fought for sport in Kansas City, so doing the same for football (and basketball) in Milan will not be unfamiliar territory.

Furthermore, alongside Cardinale, he has experience in getting the most out of TV deals, so this should help the entertainment side of the company take off as well.

Although he’s not got a background in football, the quality of his CV is undeniable and he’s thrived alongside the companies where he’s worked for years.

He’s very confident about the future, stating he’s moving on to a ‘great opportunity’ and that the opportunity of working within the MSE ‘is as big as we want it to be’, as Sportico relayed. It’s a bold statement, but he’s no stranger to delivering.

But with 5,700 away fans expected to make up a third of the crowd and much more concentrated in the away end, Slicker says their Barnsley counterparts have an important part to play, just as they did when the young team battled to win a point against Oxford United despite a ninth-minute red card for Jack Shepherd.

"I go back to the example of the Oxford game when we conceded and you feel the lift almost from the crowd and it was refreshing," says the goalkeeper. "It did give us that almost second wind.

"Whether it's the home crowd, the away crowd, I think there's a buzz from both. There might be a few beer bottles up at my head or whatever but I thrive off that (atmosphere) and I'm excited for being at both ends of the pitch.

This is Slicker's first South Yorkshire derby, and he is fully aware of its importance.

"There's a lot of (Yorkshire) derbies in League One but Sheffield Wednesday will be the big one – one of, if not the biggest, game of my career.

"It's a huge stand. We've got to make the biggest advantage of that we can."

#1958. Arsenal transfer news: David Ornstein drops interesting update on Eli Junior Kroupi ahead of January

By Lewis Blain | 18 Nov 2026 06:57

Arsenal could face imminent disappointment in their pursuit of AFC Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi, with David Ornstein providing an update on the 19-year-old's future.

The Gunners have been monitoring the Frenchman after his impressive performances, but a move for him in the January transfer window is now looking increasingly unlikely.

Ornstein has also suggested that Kroupi could favour a move away from the Premier League when he eventually leaves the Vitality Stadium.

In a recent The Athletic Q&A, Ornstein downplayed the prospect of the Cherries sanctioning a January departure, saying the club has little financial incentive to sell midway through the campaign.

The forward is under contract until 2030, meaning the Cherries are in a strong negotiating position and can afford to wait until the summer before considering significant offers.

Ornstein also highlighted that Kroupi only made his first appearance of the season on October 25th after an injury lay-off, with Bournemouth keen to benefit from his contributions during the remainder of the campaign.

Perhaps more significantly for Arsenal, the ever-reliable journalist suggested that the teenager could prefer a move abroad rather than another Premier League club.

Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona have both been heavily linked, with Ornstein indicating that the information available to him points towards those destinations being more likely than a move within England.

He did acknowledge that an exceptional financial offer from a Premier League club could change the situation, but his expectation is that Bournemouth would be more receptive to a sale next summer.

Ornstein's update represents a significant complication for Arsenal, who could now need to explore alternative attacking targets if they want to strengthen in January.

Kroupi's contract situation means Bournemouth have little reason to entertain offers, while the player's reported preference for moving abroad further weakens the Gunners' position.

Antonio Nusa could therefore become a more realistic alternative for Gunners boss Mikel Arteta.

The RB Leipzig winger is another young attacking talent attracting Premier League interest, with Arsenal previously linked alongside Tottenham and reportedly confident of competing for his signature.

Nusa would not necessarily provide the same centre-forward option as Kroupi, but his ability to operate out wide could address another area where Arsenal need greater depth.

Ultimately, Kroupi remains an exciting long-term target, but the combination of Bournemouth's stance and his apparent preference for a move abroad suggests Arsenal may have to be patient or turn their attention elsewhere in January.

#1957. Arsenal maintain perfect start but lack firepower of rivals

Bukayo Saka maintained Arsenal’s perfect start to the season, but Mikel Arteta appeared to acknowledge that the Premier League champions are in danger of leaving themselves short in attack.

There is still time for Arteta to add another forward to his squad and whether he does so or not could be important, with the transfer window closing on Tuesday night.

Having sold Leandro Trossard and with Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus on the verge of moves away, Arsenal appear light of forward options.

Lyon winger Malick Fofana has been offered to the club, but he is an underwhelming target given Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior were pursued earlier in the summer.

“We are trying to improve the squad,” Arteta, the Arsenal head coach, said. “Until Tuesday night, we’re going to try to do that. I’ve been disconnected from the world for 24 hours because I think my energy and focus has to be on the match. I will give it [my energy] now.”

Asked if he currently has enough depth in forward positions, Arteta added: “It depends if everybody is fit or not. We know that the depth has to be really big when you are fighting for four competitions. So we’re going to try to do that.”

This was an Aston Villa team there for the taking after being gutted by their Premier League rivals and still waiting for new signings to be ready to play and gel.

But Arsenal made hard work of their victory and one senses there will be more games like this if Arteta has to rely on what he has already got until at least January.

Chelsea are showing they can score goals for fun having spent £117m on Rogers. Manchester City are strengthening their firepower with the signing of Iliman Ndiaye and Bradley Barcola has joined Liverpool. Arsenal have the defence and the midfield, but not necessarily the depth of quality in forward positions of their rivals.

0.52 - Arsenal faced the fewest shots (11), the fewest shots on target (1) and allowed their opponents the lowest xG (0.52) across the first two matchdays of the Premier League season.🔒 Locked. pic.twitter.com/blSUAeqoLb

Christos Tzolis is the lone attacking signing to date and there was evidence at Villa Park that it will be a risk to rely too heavily on the Greek winger.

Tzolis had made an exciting start to his Arsenal career in the Community Shield and the first Premier League victory over Coventry City, but he had to be taken off at half-time on Monday night.

The former Club Brugge winger not only lost out to Matty Cash, but was also at the centre of Villa appeals for him to be sent off.

Tzolis had already been booked for a foul on Cash, when, in the 36th minute, he appeared to foul John McGinn as Villa broke from the edge of their own penalty area.

McGinn appealed that Tzolis should have been shown a second yellow card, but referee Jarred Gillett let the Arsenal man off the hook.

Arteta was wise to take Tzolis off at the break and his replacement, Eberechi Eze, had a hand in what proved to be Arsenal’s 59th-minute winner.

Eze slipped in Riccardo Calafiori and Saka got in front of Ian Maatsen to poke the Arsenal full-back’s low cross into the net. Saka’s goal had been the first shot on target in the game.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Just before the goal, Arsenal thought they had been awarded a penalty. Ross Barkley lost possession with a sloppy pass, allowing Declan Rice to advance towards the Villa penalty area. He played the ball through for Saka and Maatsen barged into the back of the winger.

Gillett paused before pointing to the spot, but a VAR check showed that Maatsen’s foul had taken place outside the penalty area and Martin Odegaard fired the resulting free-kick wide.

The goal and the overturned penalty were pretty much it for Arsenal in terms of threatening the hosts, for whom goalkeeper Zion Suzuki made his debut. Suzuki did not have much to do with his hands, but impressed with his distribution.

It was Villa who went closest to scoring in the first half, through one of the club’s five surviving members of last season’s Europa League-winning team.

Emiliano Buendia scored Villa’s second goal in the final against Freiburg and the Argentine rattled the Arsenal crossbar with a 20-yard shot that had beaten visiting goalkeeper David Raya.

Before then, McGinn had sent a shot over Raya’s bar and into the building site where Villa are redeveloping the club’s old North Stand.

Buendia, McGinn, Cash, Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof are the only Villa players to have started the Europa League final who have not left this summer.

Defender Ezri Konsa is one of Villa’s Europa League winners to have departed and he made his Arsenal debut as a late substitute. The defender received a mixed reception, as he was first booed by some home fans but was then applauded.

Other than hitting the bar in the opening 45 minutes, Villa squandered a chance for a quick reply to Arsenal’s opener when McGinn hesitated instead of shooting after being played in by Nicolas Jackson.

Jackson lasted 71 minutes for Villa in what proved to be a promising debut. In the first half, he raced away down the right before sending the ball across the six-yard box. But there was no team-mate on hand to convert.

One of Villa’s other summer signings, Alejandro Garnacho, is yet to make an impact for his new club. The Argentine got an earful from manager Unai Emery for not being ready to go on. He eventually replaced Ross Barkley, but could not help conjure an equaliser.

This is the start Arteta wanted. But, in attacking positions, Arsenal will finish the transfer window weaker than they started it if the club are not active in the final hours of the transfer window. And that could prove costly.

We lost. We competed well. They won the league last year. We are trying to build a team but a lot of positive things [beyond] the result. How we competed. How it was progressively better. We didn’t create clear chances. Some players made fantastic debuts. Suzuki and Jackson did very good work. I think it’s the first step forward and positive for the next matches.

Accepting this result, I think we had chances to draw the match but we are in our rebuild. It is the way [ahead for us] making these changes and I say to the supporters and players that the message is there in the way we played.

To lose one match is painful but after the pain we must try to get positive things, This is the reason I am optimistic. There are 38 matches we played two. We haven’t one point but we can get better hopefully. And we will get players [Mbaye and Harwood-Bellis].

We can feel confidence because how we want to build the team again is true, to compete like today.

I think the squad we have now is how we planned with the  players we wanted.

[Are you confident you have replaced the quality that has gone?] Yes.

I’m really happy. It’s a big win. It’s a tough place to come and earn the three points but I think we deserved it.

It was a game where 11 was not enough and the finishers came in and did a magnificent job to win it. I know how tough it is to win here.

Every big team struggles against them for the past four years because they are so good. They are well coached, have great players. Great in transition. The moment you lose the ball and let them run inside they are really dangerous but I love a lot of the things I saw from my team.

Ebs [Eze] creates the action that sees us win the game, Bruno with Mikel [Merino] in midfield changed the dynamic of it, Ezri [Konsa] really composed and calm with every decision he made and then Zubi… I’m really happy with all of them.

Every game in the Premier League it’s like [you’re saying] we have to win this game. We know the level. We know how difficult it is in this league.

[Can you sign Julian Alvarez tomorrow?] I don’t know. That’s for the people upstairs.

It was a very tough match. Aston Villa’s defensive setup made things difficult for us, constantly catching us offside. We couldn’t attack as comfortably as we did last week. But as you know, sometimes one goal is enough for us. We have a very strong defence.

Today, we were great out of possession too and didn’t allow transition attacks.

I keep my targets for myself. Every week I want to be there and try decide the game as that’s what I’m in the team to do. That’s my mentality.

[Have you seen Chelsea?] I’ve seen them. [What do you think?] We’ll see on Sunday.

Jamie Carragher explains how Arsenal broke Aston Villa down for their winning goal 🔎 pic.twitter.com/CAI8zhznrJ

Arsenal host Chelsea on Sunday at 4.30pm while Villa go to Hull City at 5.30pm on Saturday. It’s too early for a must-win game for Villa who showed some positive signs tonight but they could certainly do with one.

Arsenal win with a performance of efficiency and patience that emphasises their superiority when asked to grind out a result.

John McGinnis arguing the toss with the referee about his belief that he was fouled in the box in the dying seconds. It was outside the box and if Maatsen’s ‘tackle’ wasn’t a foul, neither was Gabriel’s.

Not sure the way of refereeing that lets a lot of calls go and waits for VAR is going to enhance the game.

Maatsen tackles Bruno Guimaraes in the Villa box with an ugly lunge in which he appears to scissor him, kicking his heel with one leg before knocking the ball away with the other but the referee deems it fair and VAR lets it pass, too.

Arsenal’s game management is working well as usual until Raya goes too long and the ball bounces through to Suzuki. But when he starts a counter-attack Alysson ends it with a dive and back come Arsenal.

Maatsen slides in late on Saka down the right, bypasses the ball and crashes into his shin. Yellow card.

Aston Villa probe but Arsenal hold them 30 yards from goal and when they do slide pass down the side of a defender for Buendia to chase, Bruno is ideally positioned to cover and make the block which he celebrates as if he were Leonardo Bonucci.

Eight minutes of stoppage time are signalled by the fourth official.

Suzuki races 15 yards outside his box to head a long pass away from Havertz to McGinn. Back come Arsenal after McGinn is squeezed off the ball but Wan-Bisska wins it back with a fine tackle. He is among the best one-on-one pure defenders in the league.

Zubimendi rattles Buendia’s bones in a crunching but legal tackle.

That was Rice’s last contribution as he limps off. He is probably OK but wise to withdraw him if he has had a twinge.

Maatsen drives down the left and cuts into the box. White leans into him, Rice guides him with a rigid left arm and the rampaging left-back loses his feet. Maatsen acknowledges Rice’s fine defending when he gets back up.

Quite a few outside observers questioned why Arsenal signed Konsa. This apparent injury to Mosquera is the reason. With Saliba out for months and Timber still struggling to regain his fitness, Mosquera was the only right-sided centre-back in the squad (unless they repurposed White, who is needed at right back).

Garnacho faces up Saka after being played down the left by Buendia but his cross is blocked by the goalscorer. Raya catches the resulting corner.

McGinn wipes out Merino from behind and is deservedly booked. Moments earlier Alysson was also booked for leaving one on Gabriel after the centre-half had cleared the ball, choosing not to put on the brakes and bodychecking him instead.

Unai Emery has just gone ballistic at substitute Alejandro Garnacho.

Emery clearly wasn’t happy with Garnacho not being ready to come on and let the Chelsea loanee know about it.

And Mosquera cannot continue having overstretched so it’s a debut for the former Villa stalwart who is greeted warmly.

Suzuki saves in a one-on-one with Havertz running through from 40 yards, waiting and refusing to go down and make things easy for Havertz, sticking up a right arm to block the shot. But he may have been offside which may mitiagte it in terms of not costing Arsenal anything but he really should have beaten the keeper.

Nice pass from Merino to set the hare running.

Barkley plays a diagonal pass across the turf out to Alysson on the right and he hares round Calafiori to cross from the byline but could not get the ball past Gabriel at the near post.

Now Maatsen goes flying but this time in the Arsenal box under a challenge from White that was a duplicate of the one 30 seconds before. ‘Premier League corrupt as f---,’ sing the Villa fans, ignoring the similarities between the two incidents. The defenders’ arms made contact with the attacking players but without the force to send them sprawling.

Havertz hits the deck in the Villa penalty area when challenged by Kamara as they fought for Odegaard’s scooped dink from the right.

Bruno Guimaraes and Mikel Merino are stripped and ready to come on.

Once again, it’s Riccardo Calafiori who opens up the opposition’s defence with his off-the-ball running. He is the one player in this Arsenal team who makes genuinely unpredictable and unexpected movements.

McGinn’s combination with Jackson looks promising and the centre-forward invites him to bullock forward down the inside-right channel with a clever pass but the Villa captain is soon swamped by yellow shirts and the ball gets stuck beneath his feet.

Gary Neville makes the fair point that one of Arsenal’s most unheralded qualities is their patience. Their confidence in their rock-solid defence does not make them reckless but they are always confident of finding a way. They trust the method implicitly.

Aston Villa 0 Arsenal 1 (Saka) Mosquera has the ball 25 yards out, left of centre, he strokes it to Eze who angles a pass to Calafiori running between Cash and Lindelof. He makes it to the byline and cuts back a low cross that Saka and Maatsen both lunge at and the Arsenal winger gets there first to turn it in.

"It's a brilliant goal, it really is" 👏 Bukayo Saka gives Arsenal the lead at Villa Park! pic.twitter.com/aV7DA8cARL

Rice, Eze and Odegaard stand over it. Rive walks away and Odegaard approaches the ball with a semi-circular run-up. He whips it over the wall and about a foot wide of the left post. Suzuki was stranded but no matter.

It was outside the box. Not all that sure it was a foul either. But Arsenal will have a free-kick.

Maatsen and Saka collide as they chase a Rice pass that Saka would never reach. Seemed to be outside the box.

It has been fairly dull fare so far as two systems and structures that cede little space clash.

Lindelof rises high to meet Rice;s dipping cross from the right as Havertz, on his shoulder, was poised to pounce. He heads it straight up and Suzuki leaps to catch it.

Now Barkley picks out a diagonal to send Jackson down the left. The centre-forward reaches the 18-yard line, cuts inside and works it over to McGinn who lofts a cross over Villa’s back-post runners and out of play.

Eze did his best work from the left last season. Villa start with Barkley scoop-chipping a pass from the middle out to the left, 40 yards upfield. Maatsen runs on to it and drives past White to ram a shot into the side-netting.

Arsenal were too slow to move the ball forward in that first half, and too loose with it when they did get into promising positions. There’s a lack of urgency in their passing. I wonder if we’ll see Bruno Guimarães soon… one of the reasons they signed him was to add more quick forward passing to their play.

Signs of encouragement for Villa without creating much while Arsenal have been stymied so far by Villa’s neutering of Tzolis and the left wing. Arsenal’s right-sided trio – White, Odegaard and Saka – look the most likely to create something.

Only a minute of added time to be played. Arsenal still lacking a spark, largely because there’s a lack of precision in their forward, line-breaking passing.

Villa will be very happy with this half. Much more like their old selves in terms of structure and organisation.

Calafiori’s throw to Gabriel is picked off by Jackson down the right and he dribbles down the right. He is forced to slow down to wait for a midfield runner. When Hemmings catches up, so have three Arsenal defenders and though Jackson bends in a low, cross to the edge of the six-yard box it is about 18 inches away from Hemmings’ reach.

Calafiori goes down in the Villa box when Pau Torres uses his arm to lever him away as they tracked the flight of a cross. The referee sees nothing wring in it and neither does VAR.

Gillett takes an age to stop the play when Cash uses his body to shove Tzolis over after the winger had played a pass. Cash obviously thinks he has rattled the new signing and is keen to rough him up some more. The ref does award a free-kick but only after that daft delay.

Tzolis loses the ball on the edge of the Villa penalty area, tackled by McGinn. The captain slots a straight pass up to Buendia who tries to bend a pass into Jackson’s stride as he sprinted down the inside right channel but Gabriel read the trajectory and got there first.

Suzuki picks out McGinn with a long pass. He feeds it to Buendia who gives Hemmings a chance to chase it down the left. Arsenal shuffle over in defence so he doubles back and returns the ball to Buendia. The No 10 whips over a dipping cross looking for Barkley and Jackson but Calafiori and Raya make sure the goalkeeper wins it.

We’ve not seen much from Christos Tzolis on Arsenal’s left wing so far. He’s been excellent since joining the club this summer but he’s hardly seen the ball in this opening half an hour and he’s just been booked after losing a battle with Matty Cash.

Arsenal free-kick 30 yards out, left of centre, for a foul on Lewis-Skelly who was artfully shielding the ball. Odegaard chips to the right post but Havertz heads it back across the box rather than going for goal and Villa clear.

Cash gets the better of Tzolis again in the tackle and then Suzuki sprays a perfect 60-yard pass out to Hemmings that Gary Neville, likening it to something Ederson was capable of delivering for Man City, one of the best goalkeeper passes he has ever seen. Tzolis was booked for stopping Cash running off with the ball.

Maatsen, who could never dislodge Digne for long, has a chance now to make the position his won. He strides down the left, exploiting Rice’s positioning error but his right-foot isn’t half as good as his left and his bending effort is scuffed far too straight and easily cleared.

Saka drives down the right after a neat Odegaard, Saka, White triangle. Pau Torres races over to toe the ball behind for a corner. Saka takes and Rice flicks it on at the near post and Suzuki tips it over. No corner, though, as Gabriel had rag-dolled McGinn at the back post after the Villa captain had backed in to him and tried to stop him making a run into the middle.

“Champions of Europe, you’ll never sing that.” Villa fans poke the wound.

Arsenal are finding it difficult to play through the middle of the pitch but have found Saka in space on the right wing on a few occasions already. Villa are congesting the central areas, where Odegaard does his best work.

Calafiori picks off Kamara’s pass looking, for the third or fourth time, to play someone, usually Jackson, in behind the left-back. A minute later Calafiori challenges McGinn for a bouncing, loose ball and stoops to use his head. colliding with McGinn’s boot. Was the head low or the boot high? Arsenal think the latter but the ref sides, rightly, with McGinn.

Arsenal corner on the left. The threat inherent every time Rice is in a quadrant diminished on this occasion because Mosquera barged Cash just after Rice struck the ball. Free-kick to Villa.

Timber may be preferred by Arteta at right-back but Saka prefers White. The two have a well-grooved partnership in tersm of who underlaps and who overlaps. They never seem to get in each other’s way.

Bukayo Saka does seem to be getting a lot of time and space on the right flank.

It’s looking a risky tactic by Villa at the moment as the England international is being invited to cut in towards the penalty area.

Havertz is played down the inside-right channel in the penalty area by a cute Odegaard pass bur he blazes his shot across goal and wide of the left post. A replay shows he was offside but even so it was a lazy finish.

Kamara grabs Tzolis round the waist from behind and when the winger hits the deck, rounds him and passus to Buendia who crashes a right-foot diagonal shot on to the bar from 20 yards. The ref did not see it as a foul despite Arsenal’s protestations but had it gone in it would have given VAR a dilemma.

Worth keeping an eye on Aston Villa midfielder George Hemmings tonight.

He is only a teenager and has emerged from Villa’s academy, but Unai Emery is already a huge fan.

Hemmings produced a highly promising performance in the Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain earlier this month.

Suzuki misjudges the flight of Rice’s typically menacing corner and flaps at it but his defenders and an offside flag leave him without egg on his face.

McGinn stops Calafiori down the left then gives the ball straight to Tzolis. The Greece winger opens his body and passes to Lewis-Skelly who shoots with his right foot from the left of the 18-yard line. Cash slides in to block the shot and it loops over the bar for a corner.

Hemmings uses his strength to hold off Ben White and shift the ball inside to McGinn who wraps his left instep around a shot and wafts it into building site behind Raya’s goal.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Taylor Harwood-Bellis are in the directors’ box watching the game. Villa don’t look like a hastily assembled team.

Suzuki knocks the ball long with his left foot, looking for Jackson but the ball spins away from him to Raya who boots it back upfield. McGinn pounces on it, turns past Rice and plays Cash in down the right. He crosses towards the near post and Mosquera hooks it clear.

Arsenal kick off with Odegaard spinning and trying to play Saka in down the right as they defend the empty North Stand end. The ball skids off the turf and Saka can’t trap it. The ball goes out for a Villa throw-in.

Who dies in the summer and played for both clubs.

Arsenal are in fact in yellow and navy. My mistake.

Villa in claret and blue with a twist, the shorts are blue for the first time since, I think 2001. Arsenal are in yellow and black. Leeds, like Arsenal, have traditionally worn yellow and blue as their away strip but have been shunted into yellow and black as well by Adidas this season.

There are a few guys standing in the North Stand with hard hats on, and it appears they are on ball retrieval duty.

They will be on red alert for any wayward shots that land in the empty stand.

Warm reception for Ezri Konsa from Villa’s fans as he walked back to the tunnel with Arsenal’s substitutes.

Konsa joined Arsenal last week for £51m, ending a spell of seven years at Villa Park.

Wonder if the likes of Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martinez will get a similar reception when they return here with Chelsea.

Aston Villa  Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Barkley; McGinn, Buendía, Hemmings; Jackson. Substitutes  Bizot, Mings, Ruggeri, Garnacho, Abraham, Bogarde, Wan-Bissaka, Edward, Lynch.

Arsenal  Raya; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Rice; Saka, Odegaard, Tzolis; Havertz. Substitutes  Arrizabalaga, Hincapié, Eze, Gyokeres, Konsa, Madueke, Merino, Zubimendi, Guimaraes.

Zion Suzuki is one of two debuts for Aston Villa tonight and there is a genuine buzz of excitement around the Japan international.

Suzuki was signed from Parma for £30m as the replacement for Emiliano Martinez and arrives with a stellar reputation.

He’s got big boots – and gloves – to fill, but Unai Emery is convinced he will become a future star at Villa Park.

The other debutant is record £65m signing Nicolas Jackson, who joined last week from Chelsea.

Good evening. Yes, the first match was not as planned but we must keep going forward. Today we are playing our first home match and I am looking forward. We need to try as soon as possible to get our best individuals fit for a good performance. And today is a good match for us. Ir is difficult but always with our supporters here we feel comfortable and confident. Hopefully we can transmit our positive energy to our supporters.

We lost the first game but it is not a [team full of rookies]. We have experienced players. They play with energy and know how we want to play. We have to adapt with Suzuki but we have confidence [in him]. Jackson, the striker, and other players, George Hemmings, he is young but played fantastically in pre-season. He knows how we want to play.

Today is a challenge but I’m really looking forward to how the players will respond collectively, individually. We know we are changing things but no excuses. We have to perform today, we have to try to adapt the new players, to build our team to get their best today.

I am positive and I am optimistic. The players are ready.

Aston Villa are in a transition period and rebuilding on and off the field.

Unai Emery’s 2.0 have been under construction all summer and there could be 10 new signings in by tomorrow morning.

Villa have of course lost six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final, with Morgan Rogers, Ollie Watkins, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Emiliano Martinez and Lucas Digne all departing this summer.

The North Stand at Villa Park, which faces the iconic Holte End, is also under renovation and closed down for tonight’s game.

It could be a bit quieter tonight but there is still a mood of optimism among Villa fans, despite such a summer of change.

We have had a real block of training sessions to work on things and prepare for this game in the right way.

We will have time to make changes throughout the game [on why he has picked an unchanged team]. They did really well [against Coventry] and for the game we expect [tonight] they have the right qualities to hurt them and that’s how we start.

They have that [upheaval in personnel] but they have been with Unai for a long time, they are a super well-coached team and we know how tough it is always to come here. We are very conscious of that but also very ambitious.

That’s the way we want to play [with aggression] constantly from the first minute, to suffocate the opponent and be better than them.

[Does it being your 250th Arsenal Premier League game add something special to it?] Just to win [makes it special].

She wore… she wore… she wore a yellow ribbon …

Two changes – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson make debuts. Joao Gomes misses the match as the first of his three-game suspension and Marco Bizot drops to the bench.

Double debuts 🤩Your Villa XI to face Arsenal this evening 👋 pic.twitter.com/Zue0ZTSJt9

Arteta names unchanged starting XI but Bruno Guimaraes is fit for the bench. Ezri Konsa joins him there.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵Unchanged for Monday night football 🔐🤝 Presented by @deel pic.twitter.com/ptvpKHDahn

In its rightful place 🏠🏆 pic.twitter.com/FMH4zve1aD

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Aston Villa and Arsenal from Villa Park. The champions travel to the team that finished fourth last season in buoyant mood and form despite some misgivings within their fanbase about their recruitment this summer.

It amounts so far to making Pier Hincapié‘s loan into a proper transfer, revamping the left wing with Christos Tzolis replacing Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli, upgrading options in central midfield by buying Bruno Guimarães and selling Cristian Norgaard – and signing Ezri Konsa from today’s opponents to give them the greatest elite defensive depth that I can recall at club since Manchester City’s Treble winners had Kyle Walker, Ruben Dias, John Stones, Nathan Aké, João Cancelo, Aymeric Laporte, Manuel Akanji, Rico Lewis and Sergio Gómez on the books at the same time.

Villa, by contrast, have endured a turbulent summer of trading with the departures of Europa League winners Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne, the aforementioned Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emi Martínez, raising, along with other departures, more than £315m. They have spent about £180m to remodel the team though Johan Manzambi, who is injured, and João Gomes, who is suspended after his red card in the 4-0 defeat by Brighton, are absent tonight.

We can expect to see Zion Suzuki, Matteo Ruggeri and hopefully Nicolas Jackson and Leon Goretzka who have been registered in time to play, plus the loan signings Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho. Still to come are the pending purchases of Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye in a process that emphasises how profoundly Villa are invested in and dependent upon their manager, Unai Emery.

After so much upheaval, it would be foolish to set much store on Villa’s 2-1 victory last season, sealed by Emi Buendía’s winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. Arsenal barely broke sweat in blowing Man City away in the Community Shield and cakewalked to victory over Coventry in the league’s opening fixture. His past work suggests Emery will be able to forge another formidable side from his talented new squad but this match feels two months too soon for him against his old club.

#1956. Jurgen Klopp gushing in praise for Arsenal star: ‘He is a complete package’

Jurgen Klopp has talked up Arsenal’s Kai Havertz as ‘a complete package as a top player’ as he hopes the forward can have a big impact for Germany.

The 27-year-old has won 64 caps for his country, scoring 25 goals, and was in action as Germany beat Serbia 3-1 on Friday.

The former Chelsea man will be in the team on Monday night for the crucial Nations League clash with Netherlands, as Klopp looks to take his side into the quarter-finals.

The Germany boss has looked to build confidence in Havertz by talking up the forward’s qualities, which he feels can match up to almost anyone in the game.

‘I have often faced teams defended by Kai, and I know very well in tactical preparations that facing Kai is not an easy task. He is a complete package as a top player,’ said Klopp.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘Mikel Arteta relies heavily on him because Kai is always reliable to put in an extraordinary performance thanks to his technical capacity and intelligence.’

He added: ‘Kai and I have agreed that there is still huge potential that we want to develop further together in the national team.’

Havertz has not been in good goal-scoring form of late, netting just once in his last 13 appearances for club and country.

That was a crucial goal in a 1-0 Arsenal win over Liverpool, but finding the back of the net has not come easily for the Gunners star.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

He will look to improve his recent record in Berlin on Monday night as Germany try and topple the group-leaders, although Klopp says the long-term project is more important than short-term success.

‘We want success right now, but the process we have set in motion takes precedence over everything else,’ he said.

‘We want to put in a top performance, then we will see how that measures up against the Netherlands.

‘We are really looking forward to this game. We wanted this opportunity, now we have got it and we want to make the most of it.

‘[Netherlands have] basically got the same squad that played at the World Cup, that is the difference between us. We are in a period of transition right now.’

AC Milan had plenty of reasons to smile after some good performances in Belgium’s game against Italy on Sunday night.

With the final Nations League games underway, Milan hoped their players would perform well to return to Milanello with confidence, and it’s fair to say they did. Indeed, Italy’s trip to Belgium provided that.

Starting with Diego Moreira, the winger performed excellently in the opener of the international break and he’s followed that up with a goal – his first for his country at a senior level – in the second game. #1954. Liverpool transfer news: Reds join Barcelona race for Brazilian defender amid Van Dijk doubt

By Axel Clody | 18 Nov 2026 07:04

Liverpool have reportedly entered the race with Barcelona to sign a Brazilian gem, with the future of Virgil van Dijk still unresolved. The Dutch defender’s contract runs until the end of the season and he has yet to reach an agreement over an extension, while Liverpool are monitoring the market.

While the January transfer window is yet to open, Liverpool are facing a dilemma behind the scenes. With his contract running until the end of the season, Van Dijk has no renewal agreement in progress and can sign a pre-contract agreement from January.

With the situation of the Dutch defender unresolved, Liverpool have entered the race with Barcelona to sign a Brazilian gem.

According to Sports Illustrated, Liverpool have sent scouts to follow the rise of Arthur Dias closely and are now assessing the possibility of buying him from Athletico Paranaense. The 19-year-old defender is one of the breakout stars of Brazilian football in 2026 and is being watched by several European clubs.

Barcelona’s interest in Arthur Dias is long-standing, as being left-footed and comfortable playing out from the back are qualities missing from manager Hansi Flick’s squad. Van Dijk, who is right-footed but also plays on the left side of central defence, would leave a gap for Liverpool to fill should he depart.

The Brazilian centre-back has a contract until December 2028 and has already seen a Tottenham Hotspur offer of £18m (€21m) rejected by Athletico Paranaense. The club’s board believes Arthur Dias should only be released for an offer of at least £25.5m (€30m) because of his high potential.

So far, Liverpool have made no formal approach to Athletico Paranaense for the young defender, but the competition is not limited to Barcelona.

Clubs such as Bayer Leverkusen and RB Leipzig are also monitoring Arthur Dias, who gained international visibility with his first two call-ups to the Brazil national team in the post-World Cup international breaks.

Brazilian aside, Liverpool’s number four has no guaranteed future at Anfield. Despite his idol status and undisputed place in the starting line-up under manager Andoni Iraola, Van Dijk has no advanced talks with the club’s directors over his stay, with moves towards an extension expected to gather pace at the turn of the year.

The captain himself admitted in a recent interview that he plans to stay at Liverpool, but has no news on his situation.

The Spanish manager is in favour of Van Dijk staying, as the Dutchman is not only a leadership figure in the dressing room but also a pillar of the defensive system, having won 75% of his duels in this season’s Premier League.

In that context, AC Milan have emerged as one of the clubs interested in the 35-year-old defender. According to Gazzetta dello Sport, Milan owner Gerry Cardinale is an admirer of the Dutchman and believes he can make a difference to Ruben Amorim’s project through his experience and technical quality.
