#1910. When are the 2026-27 Nations League quarter-finals? Dates, fixtures, teams, how they qualified

By Matt Law | 18 Nov 2026 11:54, Last updated: 18 Nov 2026 11:57

The 2026-27 UEFA Nations League quarter-finals will take place in March 2027.

The draw for the final eight will take place on November 20, 2026, where it will be decided which teams will face off against each other for a spot in the semi-finals.

Here, Sports Mole runs through all of the details surrounding next year's matches, including dates, fixtures and how each of the eight teams booked a spot in the quarter-finals.

The first legs of the respective last-eight contests will take place between March 25 and March 27, 2027, with the second legs occurring between March 28 and March 30, 2027.

The draw for the quarter-finals of the 2026-27 Nations League will take place at 11am UK time on November 20 at UEFA's headquarters.

Finishing first in the section means that home advantage is gained for the second leg, while the winners of each group will take on a runner-up from another section.

France, Germany, England and Portugal have been the group winners, with Belgium, Netherlands, Spain and Norway qualifying as runners-up in each section.

Portugal are the holders of the Nations League trophy and also the most successful side in the history of the competition, having won it twice (2019 and 2025).

Spain (2023) and France (2021) have also won the tournament.

Germany, England, Belgium, Netherlands and Norway could become first-time winners of the Nations League in 2026-27, with the final set to take place in June 2027.

France finished first in Group A1 to secure a spot in the quarter-finals of the tournament, claiming 13 points from their six matches, boasting a record of four wins, one draw and one defeat.

Belgium were second in Group A2, one point behind the section winners France, having claimed 12 points from their six games, boasting a record of four wins and two defeats from six games.

Germany finished at the top of Group A2 with 11 points from six matches. Incredibly, each of Germany, Netherlands and Greece had 11 points from six games, but Germany finished at the summit on UEFA''s head-to-head goal difference tiebreaker.

Netherlands managed to sneak second spot in Group A2 ahead of Greece on overall goal difference, with Xavi's team finishing with a record of three wins, two draws and one defeat from six matches.

England spectacularly secured first position in Group A3 courtesy of their standout 3-2 success over Spain in Madrid on Sunday night; the Three Lions won five and lost one of their six games to collect 15 points, and they ultimately had a better overall goal difference.

Spain were bumped back down to second spot in Group A3 due to their loss to England; the reverse to the Three Lions proved to be their first defeat in 90 minutes since March 2024.

Portugal finished at the top of Group A4, boasting 15 points from their six matches, in order to comfortably secure a position in the quarter-finals of the tournament.

Norway managed to sneak into second spot in Group A4 ahead of Denmark on the final matchday, recording a 3-2 success over the Danes, which gave them the advance in the head-to-head tiebreaker.

#1908. Wes Brown: ‘Man Utd still have every chance of Champions League qualification’

Wes Brown believes Manchester United should still be aiming for a top-five finish this season after Mauricio Pochettino was appointed head coach.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss has officially taken the reins at Old Trafford after his final two matches with the United States national team.

Pochettino has undoubtedly been thrown in at the deep end, with United winless in their last eight Premier League matches and facing Liverpool in his first game on Sunday.

But former Red Devils defender Brown believes that the Argentine has the quality to inspire a quick turnaround from his new crop of players.

‘Poch is very experienced, and he has his own style of play, but it’s all about consistency, he told Metro. ‘Making the players believe they’re good enough and making sure they do it week in, week out.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘We’ve had no momentum; we’ve played well here and there in games, and when we did we managed to score, but at the same time we’ve been very poor at times and open to teams scoring at will, making loads of mistakes.

‘The confidence isn’t there, but he’ll be coming in and just trying to get consistency through the team.

‘When a new manager comes in, the players really make an effort, that’s just the way it goes, but then it’s up to the manager to keep that going through the season, and whether or not he’ll be able to, we’ll all have to see.’

Pochettino brings with him extensive experience in the Premier League but also a proven track record of nurturing young talent into the first team.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

And Brown is hopeful that academy duo Shea Lacey and Harry Amass could benefit from the Argentine’s arrival, adding: ‘If anyone, you think those two might come in and get a game under the new manager to show what they can do.

‘I think at the moment, you are looking at Shea Lacey and thinking, “Yeah, he can get a game”. He delivers, he runs, he works hard.

Pochettino faces a trip to Anfield for his first game in charge (Picture: Getty)

‘But I also think when you’re in a position where you don’t necessarily just bring in the young lads as well. I think that’s a tough gig if I’m being honest, and you can’t just bring them in when the team’s like this.’

Pochettino will have to endure a frenetic start to life in the United dugout, with a run of eight games in 21 days starting at Anfield on Sunday.

But with plenty of the season still ahead, Brown thinks United should still be aiming high if they can start fast under their seventh permanent boss since Alex Ferguson’s retirement.

‘There’s still a chance of getting into Europe, 100 per cent,’ Brown added.

‘Even though it’s been very disappointing, even if you look at the table now, the gap is not that big. It’s maybe 8-9 points from a European place, if that.

‘So you’ve still got to have that in the back of your mind. It’s Manchester United; that’s where you aim to be, if not higher, and I’m sure Poch will definitely be looking to get us in that sort of area and going in that direction.’

#1907. Andriy Shevchenko demands apology from Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk over ‘baseless’ failed drugs test claims

Andriy Shevchenko has demanded an apology from Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk after he blamed Ukraine’s national team for his failed drugs test.

Mudryk, who is on loan at Tottenham Hotspur from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after he tested positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old initially faced a four-year ban but returned to football this summer after he accepted that he had breached anti-doping rules and agreed to a suspension equal to the time he had already served.

Speaking to YouTube channel Guest of Gordon this week, Mudryk was asked who he felt was to blame for the adverse finding.

‘The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team,’ Mudryk said.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

‘It should never have existed. I probably haven’t said it publicly yet but I’m saying it now.

‘I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.’

Asked how meldonium got into his system, Mudryuk said: ‘The Ukrainian national team has absolutely no security system. At clubs, when you travel to an away game, there are always people responsible for what happens on the hotel floors and in the team.

‘There are people who keep an eye on it. In the Ukrainian national team we have a nutritionist who hands us pills every couple of days before games. He brings us a little cup. Everyone has to take the pills that are in that cup.’

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Former Chelsea striker Shevchenko, who is now the president of the Ukrainian Association of Football, has hit back at Mudryk’s claims and has described the winger’s version of events as ‘baseless slander’.

‘I want to express my position on the accusations of Mykhailo Mudryk. Loud statements were made about the UAF, the Ukrainian national team. This is a baseless slander against our people, who do their job honestly and professionally,’ Shevchenko said in a statement to Tribuna Ukraine.

‘Instead, after the suspension of Mykhailo Mudryk, his representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to artificially find an employee who would take responsibility for the appearance of meldonium in his doping sample.

‘The UAF refused – such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work. The accusations from Mykhailo’s representatives were not confirmed or proven after many studies and inspections. The investigation and the final settlement agreement with WADA and the English association confirm this.

‘After Mykhailo became a Chelsea player, the club sent a letter to the UAF requesting that he not be given any medication during the national team training camp. The team staff complied with this request.

‘Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also agreed for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him during the training camp. These people monitored his regimen and recovery and helped him with his daily life.

‘The UAF has completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk’s representatives with the information they requested and have been in contact with those who worked on the case.

‘I know people who have been working in the national team for many years. I trust them, because during all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make one doubt their professionalism

‘If Mykhailo has evidence to support his words, let him provide it. If there is no such evidence, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he questioned.’

#1906. Former Rangers striker Peter van Vossen on THAT Old Firm miss 30 years ago today... 'I wasn't paying attention and the ball hit my shin, but I still blame Jorg Albertz!'

Published: 09:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:44 EST, 14 November 2026

In a career spanning almost 20 years, Peter van Vossen won the Champions League, made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup with his country and won league titles in both the Netherlands and Scotland.

Point being, it’s reductive to define his time in football by one excruciating miss. But here we are.

It’s 30 years to the day since Van Vossen missed an open goal for Rangers during a crucial Old Firm clash at Celtic Park. Leading 1-0 and with less than seven minutes remaining, the Dutch forward had a chance to seal all three points for the nine-in-a-row-chasing Light Blues. Instead, he blazed over with the goal at his mercy.

In the decades since, the spurned chance has become the benchmark by which all other misses have been measured. ‘Sure, it was bad — but was it “Van Vossen” bad?’

The man himself has seldom spoken about the events of that powder keg of a night. Until now. Living the quiet life in rural Holland, Van Vossen has given Daily Mail Sport a full account of his professional nadir.

‘I mostly remember being mad at Jorg [Albertz],’ he says. ‘I was seriously p***** off with him. Paul Gascoigne played a pass inside to me and I clipped a first-time ball in behind the Celtic defence, who were pressing high. If Jorg had just left it, I was one-on-one with the goalie and I would have fancied my chances.

Rangers striker Peter van Vossen sends the ball skywards in a crucial Old Firm clash in 1996

‘I also thought there was a chance he might have been offside, so when you see me running through and stretching out my arms, that’s not me telling him that we’re through; that’s me telling him to leave it and get out of the way!

‘Anyway, he didn’t, I continued my run, he passed it to me and, because I was still livid when the ball arrived at me, I wasn’t paying enough attention. It took a bit of a bobble, I ended up basically hitting it with my shin and, yeah, it unfortunately flew over the bar.’

To his relief, Rangers held on for a 1-0 win to leapfrog their bitter rivals at the top of the table, albeit only after Andy Goram saved a Pierre van Hooijdonk penalty awarded moments after Van Vossen’s horror miss.

‘Walter Smith came up to me in the dressing room afterwards and said, “It’s just as well The Goalie saved that penalty otherwise I’d have f****** killed you!”’ smiles Van Vossen.

‘It was horrible but I can laugh about it now because we won the game. I wish I had scored but I didn’t, so there’s nothing I can do except try to find the humour in it.’

Van Vossen signed for Rangers in January 1996 in a swap deal that saw Oleg Salenko join Istanbulspor. He came with some pedigree, too, having won the Champions League with Ajax in 1995, a year after featuring for the Netherlands on their run to the last eight of the World Cup in the US.

At that time, Rangers, bankrolled by David Murray, were in the throes of a project designed to deliver European glory, while maintaining their dominance of Scottish football. Those two objectives, says Van Vossen, were misaligned.

‘We had a quality group of players that was far better than anything else in Scotland at the time,’ he says. ‘That made us incredibly difficult to beat in the league. But when we went into European games, we were exposed. The lack of competition in the league along with the lifestyles of some of our players was not compatible with taking on champions from other countries.

‘I always felt like we were technically a little behind. Our training usually consisted of a warm-up, a game of football, and a warm-down. That was a big adjustment for me. At Ajax, we played in a system and we worked hard on making sure everybody knew their role. In Scotland, it seemed like there was no real system. You could run anywhere you wanted. I don’t really think I learned anything in my time there.’

That’s not to say he didn’t enjoy his two-and-a-half years in Glasgow. Quite the opposite.

‘I loved playing for Rangers,’ he says. ‘Particularly that second season [1996/97]. I started really well and scored seven or eight goals in the first handful of games. I remember people being quite surprised because I had taken some time to settle. They would joke, “Who are you, Van Vossen’s better twin brother?” But I loved it.’

A dejected Van Vossen can't believe he's missed in a moment that would follow him forever

He reserves particular affection for Walter Smith. ‘He was a fantastic manager and a true gentleman,’ he nods. ‘He helped me through a difficult time in my personal life. When I wasn’t in his team on the weekend, for example, I would ask him if I could go back to the Netherlands to see my children. He always said yes on the condition that I was back in time for training at 10am on Monday.

‘He genuinely cared about his players. I remember Vitesse being interested in bringing me back to Holland and their coach Leo Beenhakker coming to watch me at Ibrox.

‘After the game, he found Walter and said, “We want to sign Peter, but we think £300,000 is too much”. Walter said to him, “Listen to me carefully. We don’t do business like this. First, you and I will go for a lunch, have a respectful chat and only when we’ve got to know each other, that’s when we’ll talk about money”.

‘Walter came to me afterwards and said, “Look, I know you’re not playing as much as you would like but I won’t let you sign for him. This isn’t a good manager and I can’t allow it. You’re one of my players and I care about getting you the right move, not just any move”. I really respected that.’

Van Vossen endured a much more difficult relationship with Smith’s assistant Archie Knox, a man he describes as ‘manipulative’.

‘I didn’t get on with him,’ he says. ‘People talk a lot nowadays about creating a safe space and the right culture in workplaces. To me, Archie didn’t do that. He was always shouting, always right on top of you, in your face, kicking bottles. He behaved like a madman.

Van Vossen scored nine goals in 31 caps for the Netherlands between 1992 and 2000

‘At Ajax, the coaches wanted to know how you were feeling. They understood that being well mentally was as important as being physically fit. Archie wasn’t interested in that. He was always aggressive, but only with the players he didn’t like. He had his favourites. If you weren’t one of them, he made sure you knew all about it.’

Background tensions aside, Van Vossen’s first full season at Ibrox, 1996/97, has assumed a special place in Rangers’ folklore. They finished five points clear of Celtic to equal their rivals’ record of nine consecutive league titles, having laid the foundations with four league wins out of four over Tommy Burns’ side.

Despite his famous miss being the closest he ever came to scoring in an Old Firm clash, Van Vossen insists he relished those occasions.

‘I loved those games,’ he says. ‘The atmosphere, home and away, was unbelievable and the quality of the players on the pitch was outstanding. To be honest, there wasn’t a whole lot of football played. There were lots of mistakes, fights and loads of running. I remember feeling tired after just ten minutes. I wasn’t built for that kind of pace! But they were great to be part of.

‘The week of Old Firm matches, you could feel the pressure building. I remember being in Glasgow city centre one day and I needed a taxi. I waved one down but when it pulled up, the driver must have been a Celtic fan because he raised his middle finger and swore at me before driving away. Whereas, with Rangers taxi drivers, it was the opposite. I honestly think they would have driven me around Scotland for free.

Van Vossen had a spell in charge of Fortuna Sittard but now labels himself a 'house husband'

‘That’s just what football is like in Glasgow. It’s on a whole other level to anything else. I’ve played in big derbies in the Netherlands and Turkey. Believe me, nothing comes close to the Old Firm.’

After finding his playing time limited as Rangers pursued ten-in-a-row, Van Vossen was relieved to learn that his old international manager, Dick Advocaat, would take over from Smith in time for the 1998/99 season. His joy, however, was short-lived when Murray used him as a makeweight in a transfer for Feyenoord midfielder Giovanni van Bronckhorst.

‘David Murray was a brilliant guy, but he made a huge mistake when he tried to sell me to Feyenoord behind the back of Dick Advocaat,’ says Van Vossen. ‘Dick was taking over and he was keen for me to be part of his plans.

‘I remember he was flying from Amsterdam to Glasgow when he phoned me to talk about some of his ideas. I said, “Dick, I’m sorry, but I think I’m joining Feyenoord. The deal is almost done”. He told me to stay put and said that when he got to Glasgow, he and I were going to go and see Murray.

‘I remember Dick said to him, “How can you sell players behind my back? I need to be involved in these conversations”. Murray said, “You’re absolutely right, I apologise”. He handed me a blank cheque and said, “Peter, write down whatever number you want to stay. It’s not a problem”.

‘But I couldn’t do it. I respected him for apologising to Dick, but I had lost confidence in him. I couldn’t play for somebody who would do something like that.

Van Vossen scored 11 goals in his 36 appearances for Rangers between 1996 and 1998

‘I took a 60 per cent drop in wages to join Feyenoord but they were the team I had supported as a boy and I needed to be somewhere I was wanted and where I was being treated with respect.’

Although his spell at Ibrox ended on a slightly sour note, Van Vossen recalls it fondly. ‘It was a family,’ he says. ‘Everybody had a part to play, from the players on the pitch to the ladies in the kitchen. I mean, they were incredible. I remember being on a ferry one time and I got chatting to a truck driver who told me he sold flowers. We had a good conversation and exchanged numbers.

‘When I got back to Glasgow, I got in touch with him and said, “Can you do me a favour? Can you deliver ten bouquets of flowers to Ibrox?” Sure enough, this huge truck pulled up outside the ground one day, with something like ten thousand flowers in the back. They pulled out ten bouquets and delivered them to the ladies in the kitchen. They were delighted, but it was the least I could do. They treated you like one of their own. Like I say, we were one big family.’

These days, the head of that family is one of Van Vossen’s old teammates, Derek McInnes, and he’s backing him to deliver silverware.

Despite carving out a successful career, Van Vossen is remembered primarily for THAT miss

‘I remember Derek well,’ he says. ‘Like me, he didn’t play every game, but he always gave 100 per cent and I expect he’ll be the same as a manager. He’s a people person and I imagine he is a fantastic man-manager. I have no doubt he’ll do a great job.’

Having dabbled in management and punditry since hanging up his boots, Van Vossen now describes himself as a ‘house husband’ who dotes on wife Jojanneke and his stepchildren Sem, Lilly, Madée and Eva. He’s also currently writing his autobiography. The simple pleasures, he insists, are what matter most to him.

‘I don’t need to have lots of expensive things and a certain kind of lifestyle to be a rich man,’ he adds. ‘I’m a rich man because of the memories I have and the good times I enjoyed as a footballer.

‘If I close my eyes, I can still remember what it was like to run onto the pitch at Ibrox in front of 50,000 supporters, and it gives me goosebumps. I am very fortunate to have had that opportunity.’

Manchester United are reportedly prepared to take legal action over JJ Gabriel's proposed move to Real Madrid if they uncover any evidence of inducement.

Gabriel revealed back in September that he wanted to leave Old Trafford after failing to break into the senior team.

Although he remains registered with the club until the end of the season, that would not prevent him from moving elsewhere in the European Union once he turns 16.

A host of clubs were interested in signing the youngster, but it now appears that he is set to join Real Madrid.

Gabriel posted a farewell message to Man Utd supporters, thanking the club for their role in his development, but the Red Devils are understood to be angered by his decision.

According to the Manchester Evening News, the Red Devils were disappointed that the video was posted without any prior contact from Gabriel's representatives.

Man Utd have reportedly made several attempts to check on the teenager's welfare since he requested to leave, but have been unable to establish contact with his family.

Meanwhile, agency Epic Sports has become Gabriel's new representative, with the club believing that the youngster has been poorly advised by his father throughout the process.

The Red Devils are prepared to explore every available legal avenue should evidence of inducement from Madrid emerge, given the strict regulations surrounding the recruitment of players under the age of 18.

The youngster only turned 16 on October 6, and there was little reason to believe that his pathway to the first team would have been blocked at Old Trafford.

Critics may argue that Man Utd could have handled his development better, perhaps following Barcelona's approach with Lamine Yamal, although such success stories are relatively rare.

What appears particularly surprising is Gabriel's decision to join Real Madrid, where he would face competition from the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior, Arda Guler, Endrick and Yan Diomande for a place in the senior side.

Man Utd can hardly be held solely responsible for his decision, but the way this saga has unfolded could raise questions about the club's ability to retain and nurture its most promising young talents.

#1899. Chelsea news: Manager merry-go-round exposes flaws of BlueCo model at Strasbourg

By Axel Clody | 18 Nov 2026 12:46

Has Strasbourg become a prisoner of BlueCo’s strategy? The departure of Hugo Oliveira, replaced by Vitor Matos after only a few months in the dugout, has reignited questions over the management of the Alsatian club.

Only 13th in Ligue 1 with 10 points after 10 games, Strasbourg are going through a very difficult start to the season. But beyond the results, it is above all the absence of continuity that stands out. Since January, four managers have followed one another in the Strasbourg dugout. Such instability is hard to reconcile with building a genuine sporting project.

Liam Rosenior’s departure for Chelsea last January had already given a glimpse of the limits of the model. The Englishman, now at Paris FC, had established a playing identity and allowed Strasbourg to rediscover a certain ambition, before being called up to the flagship club of the BlueCo galaxy.

Gary O’Neil succeeded him, before joining Ipswich Town a few months later. Hugo Oliveira, who arrived this summer, ultimately lasted only four months. Vitor Matos is now expected to succeed him.

This succession of changes raises an obvious question: how do you build a team when its manager changes so regularly?

Each coach arrives with his own principles, tactical preferences and recruitment needs. Rosenior’s high press, O’Neil’s orientations and Oliveira’s intentions have not allowed lasting continuity to be established. Strasbourg’s players constantly have to adapt, while collective automatisms are called into question.

The transfer window does not help matters. Strasbourg had a particularly busy summer, with a multitude of movements, including several players from the Chelsea ecosystem.

The club sometimes looks more like a piece in a vast player circulation system than one building its squad around clearly identified needs. Strasbourg’s sporting logic therefore seems regularly to come second to that of BlueCo.

It would be unfair, though, to deny the benefits of this policy: Strasbourg have rediscovered a European dimension and reached the semi-finals of the Conference League in spring 2026. The club also has a young squad with resale value, and has the resources to attract promising talent.

But what is the point of developing players if the best of them are liable to leave as soon as an opportunity arises within the group? What is the point of investing in a manager if he can be replaced so quickly?

Rosenior’s departures and the player movements between Strasbourg and Chelsea illustrate this difficulty in preserving a trajectory of the club’s own.

BlueCo has found in Alsace a tremendous breeding ground for its young talents. But Strasbourg cannot be reduced to a development centre at the service of Chelsea.

The French club’s supporters expect a team to identify with, a readable project and ambitions that do not change with the owner’s needs. By treating Strasbourg as an interchangeable element of its organisation, BlueCo risks weakening exactly what gives the club its value: its identity. Unless it is already too late? Strasbourg would benefit from disengaging from this stifling structure.

#1896. The four problems Mauricio Pochettino needs to fix at Man United: From big names causing unrest in the dressing room to an issue which plagued Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick before him, these are the items top of his Old Trafford in-tray

Published: 21:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 10:51 EST, 14 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino will see out his final two games as US national team boss with a double-header against Haiti before starting work at Manchester United on Wednesday.

The 54-year-old won’t have any time to waste with a daunting first game against United’s bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday followed by a European clash with Sporting Lisbon in Portugal three days later.

With United languishing in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League standings, it’s clear why Pochettino has been brought in to replace Michael Carrick on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Daily Mail Sport looks at the most pressing matters in Pochettino’s in-tray at Carrington as the former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss and his backroom staff head for Manchester...

Mauricio Pochettino is the new manager of Manchester United - but the problems he has to fix are already piling up

It sounds obvious, but winning games to get United out of the Premier League drop zone has to be the first priority.

Everything at a football club flows from the results on the pitch, and United’s humiliating decline this season has had ramifications throughout Old Trafford and Carrington.

The players are clearly low on confidence which has only exacerbated the team’s dismal performances and brought just one win in 10 Premier League games, against newly-promoted Ipswich – United’s worst start in 40 years.

Diogo Dalot is a prime example, after fans cheered his substitution in the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa last weekend, and the defender cut a crestfallen figure as he left Old Trafford to go on international duty with Portugal.

The Stretford End also turned on the players as the atmosphere turned toxic after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth at the end of last month, having vented their anger towards the club’s ownership – the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – as well as chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox at every opportunity.

That won’t go away anytime soon, but a winning team will at least take some of the sting out of the situation if appointing Pochettino can give United a ‘bounce’ and divert attention back onto the pitch.

United players are low on confidence, not least Diogo Dalot (left) whose substitution was cheered by his own fans against Aston Villa

The United team were also lambasted by the Stretford End after the 3-0 loss to Bournemouth last month

Carrick enjoyed a good start, losing just two of his 17 games in charge in the second half of last season to earn a two-year contract, but United struggled under him this term due to a combination of poor recruitment, injuries and lack of fitness.

These are all issues that Pochettino must try to put right. There is little he can do about recruitment until the January transfer window opens and United have a chance to atone for their mistake in not signing cover at left back and centre forward last summer, which backfired spectacularly when both Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko picked up injuries.

He can, however, try to get more out of United’s £155million midfield signings Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again – Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, and a United squad that was good enough to finish third in the Premier League last season.

Injuries have been a major problem with the hamstring strain that will keep Baleba out of action for Pochettino’s first few weeks in charge just the latest setback.

As well as Shaw, Sesko, Baleba and long-term casualty Manuel Ugarte, United have also lost Amad Diallo, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Lisandro Martinez, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui for parts of this season.

Pochettino must get more out of United’s £155million midfield signing Carlos Baleba – once he is fit again

United have struggled to keep up with their opponents since the opening day - a lack of fitness has plagued every manager since Ole Gunnar Solskjaer

The good news for Pochettino is that Shaw and Rashford are hoping to be fit for Anfield, while Matthijs de Ligt is available again after a year out with back problems. However, Sesko’s absence until the new year leaves the new boss without his most natural source of goals.

Fitness is another matter and United have looked short of it since the opening-day defeat at Hull City amid concerns that the coaching levels dropped off under Carrick and were too relaxed.

They covered 120.8 kilometres against Villa – the most in a league game under Carrick – and Pochettino will demand that and a whole lot more as he increases the work-rate among his new squad.

It’s a problem that has hindered a succession of United bosses going back to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and the Argentine must find a way to drill a better work ethic into United.

The problems at United this season have inevitably led to unrest in the dressing room, with the biggest issue centred around captain Bruno Fernandes.

News that Fernandes has rejected United’s latest contract offer has come as no surprise given his dramatic change in fortunes from last season, and Pochettino must find a way to get arguably United’s best player back in form and onside.

Having set a new Premier League record for assists and picked up a string of player of the year awards last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off a cliff as he struggled with an injury sustained at the World Cup, and he suffered the rare indignity of being benched for the loss to Bournemouth.

Never one to hide his mood very well, the 32-year-old criticised Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat by Como in what was a major blow to his head coach.

Never one to hide his mood very well, Bruno Fernandes has been disgruntled of late and rejected United's offer of a new contract

Lisandro Martinez looks to be headed for the exit door - although the arrival of his fellow Argentine Pochettino may help things

While the United hierarchy will try to persuade Fernandes to sign a new deal in keeping with their reduced wage structure and the fact he will turn 33 next year, Pochettino has to find a way of relighting the fire in his skipper.

Whether the club will make as much effort to keep Lisandro Martinez as he comes towards the end of his contract remains to be seen after another member of United’s leadership team took aim at Wilcox’s recruitment after the defeat by Atletico Madrid. It is said to have caused an angry clash between Martinez and summer signing Tielemans on the way back from Spain.

Martinez looks to be heading for the Old Trafford exit, but it will be interesting to see if the arrival of his compatriot Pochettino – a combative Argentine centre back in much the same mould as a player – has an impact on that.

As a former defender, Pochettino won’t need telling that leaking 15 goals in the last five games simply isn’t good enough. United have now let in 30 in all competitions this season, the most of any club in Europe’s top five leagues apart from Lens.

They have been appalling at the back, conceding in the opening seconds to Atletico, Como and Villa. Had they been able to hold out and prevent late equalisers against Everton and Tottenham, the additional four points would have them 12th in the table rather than in the relegation zone.

A revolving door of makeshift left backs in the absence of Shaw and Dorgu, De Ligt’s belated comeback and Martinez’s needless red card at Chelsea haven’t helped.

Goalkeeper Senne Lammens, so composed last season, looks considerably more shaky behind a leaky and ever-changing back-four, and had arguably his worst game against Villa last weekend.

Pochettino couldn’t ask for a tougher first test than going to Anfield, and knows that United will have to start by being solid at the back.

#1895. Liverpool injury update: Virgil van Dijk, Giovanni Leoni, Jeremie Frimpong latest news and return dates

Liverpool have been handed a double defensive boost ahead of the Premier League clash with Manchester United.

It has been a mixed international break for Andoni Iraola’s side on the injury front, with concerns over Virgil van Dijk and Dominik Szoboszlai.

However, there was some positive news, as star striker Alexander Isak was rested by Sweden on Tuesday night, meaning he should be fully fresh and raring to go on Sunday afternoon.

With that in mind, here is the latest Liverpool injury news and return dates…

Leoni is one of two Liverpool players reported by The Athletic to have returned to first team training after a long injury lay-off.

The Italian has missed a full year of action since suffering an ACL injury, with further issues in his knee. Originally pencilled for a September return, the complications have pushed Leoni’s comeback to December.

Head coach Iraola explained: “It’s taking more time than we wanted. The planning was to train with the team in this past international break [but] probably it’s going to be in the next international break, so we’ve lost one month in the process.

“Giovanni’s injury, I wasn’t here but talking to the medical department, it was not just an ACL – it was a bad injury, a lot of things around the knee were involved apart from the ACL.”

However, despite a return to training, it is expected that Leoni is still a few weeks away from being in contention for some playing time.

Potential return date: Saturday December 12, vs Leeds (H)

Conor Bradley is the other long-term absentee back in first-team training. The Northern Ireland international suffered bone and ligament damage in his knee against Arsenal in January.

Bradley was predicted to resume training with the first team during the international break, implying that he is keeping pace with his expected recovery.

Potential return date: Wednesday, December 2 vs Sunderland (H)

Van Dijk dropped out of the Netherlands’ squad for Nations League clashes with Greece and Germany, with the defender’s absence explained as fitness reasons.

“The Ryan Gravenberch thing is a day-to-day thing, it’s a matter of pain. Let’s see if he can deal with the pain and he can help us.”

Potential return date: Sunday November 22, vs Manchester United (H)

One of four Dutch players in the Liverpool squad, Jeremie Frimpong also missed out on representing his country during the latest international break.

There was small hope that the right wing-back would have been available for the Crystal Palace, but another two weeks of recovery and Frimpong might be able to make his return against United.

Iraola said:“Frimpong is obviously a new muscle injury and it happened, I think, in the second or third minute he was playing, difficult to predict and we will have to wait until he recovers.

“But it’s going to be difficult, I think, before the [November international] break. We will try but it’s going to be difficult to have him.”

Potential return date: Sunday November 22, vs Manchester United (H)

The Frenchman has not played since his Achilles injury against Paris Saint-Germain last season, missing the World Cup.

In June it was reported by L’Equipe that the striker is targeting a return at Christmas time, with Liverpool’s trip to Hull in his sights.

To the surprise of many, Ekitike was included in Iraola’s squad for the Champions League league phase, highlighting the hope that he would be available for the final two games in January, against Inter Milan and Lens.

#1894. Aston Villa transfer news: Unai Emery 'interested' in midfielder with 155 Chelsea appearances

By Darren Plant | 18 Nov 2026 12:53

Aston Villa have reportedly identified AC Milan midfielder Ruben Loftus-Cheek as a potential winter transfer target.

Earlier on Wednesday, Villa announced that one of their current engine-room options had penned a new long-term contract.

Unai Emery is also not short of players for that position, with Boubacar Kamara, Joao Gomes, Leon Goretzka and Ross Barkley earning regular minutes.

Nevertheless, not helped by the inconsistent performances and individual mistakes of some of those aforementioned players, Villa remain off the pace in the Premier League.

According to Calciomercato, Loftus-Cheek has emerged as a possible option for the turn of the year.

The report alleges that Villa Park is viewed as a 'potential destination' for the former Chelsea midfielder.

Loftus-Cheek contributed 13 goals and 18 assists from his 155 appearances in a Blues shirt, but he has been at San Siro since the summer of 2023.

His stint at AC Milan can be viewed as a relative success, with 13 goals and four assists coming from 109 outings for the Italian giants.

However, the 11-cap England international's contract is due to expire at the end of the season, putting him in a position where he could leave on a free transfer in the summer.

Milan are open to cashing in on the 30-year-old in order to free up transfer funds and space on their wage bill.

Ruben Amorim's side have also won their last two matches against Inter Milan and Genoa, games which Loftus-Cheek missed through injury.

Despite Loftus-Cheek possessing qualities that Emery arguably lacks within his squad, a move to Villa makes little sense for the player.

Villa already have too many options in the number six, eight and 10 positions in Emery's familiar 4-2-3-1 or 4-4-1-1 formations.

Although Tammy Abraham has been linked with an exit from Villa, it seems unlikely that Loftus-Cheek would transition into a backup number nine behind Nicolas Jackson and Brian Madjo at this point of his career.

#1893. Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

Sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

“I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”

Gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

“We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

Monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a big opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car company makes sense, despite what I said earlier.

Sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

The Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6

I’m as big a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

“What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton said yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

#1892. Transfer news LIVE: Vinicius to Arsenal; Nusa bid; Man Utd plot Paz talks; Chelsea, Liverpool latest

The January transfer window is fast approaching, with Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham all looking to strengthen their squads ahead of the second half of the season. Arsenal are among the clubs interested in Como midfielder Nico Paz, although they face competition from Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain. Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi and RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa are also on the Gunners’ radar, while Vinicius Junior has reportedly emerged as a target once again.

Mauricio Pochettino officially begins his tenure as Manchester United manager today and could make Calvin Bassey his first signing. The former Chelsea boss is keen to shore up a defence that has struggled this season, with the Fulham defender potentially offering a solution. Pochettino is also set to face the media ahead of United’s meeting with Liverpool as preparations continue.

Chelsea are confident of securing a deal for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott when the window opens, despite the Cherries insisting he is not for sale. Liverpool are also monitoring Mexican youngster Gilberto Mora, while the Reds are now leading the race for Lamine Camara, who came close to joining Chelsea on deadline day in the summer. Follow all the latest transfer news, rumours and gossip live below!

Fulham are in talks with captain Calvin Bassey over a new contract as they look to fend off interest from Manchester United, writes Standard Sport’s Sam Tabuteau.

The 26-year-old centre-back, whose contract expires next summer, is understood to be on United’s shortlist as they look to sign defensive reinforcements in January.

Fulham hold the option to extend Bassey’s current deal by a further year.

The Cottagers are keen to keep hold of Bassey, especially after Alvaro Arbeloa promoted him to captain in the summer.

Nothing has been agreed yet, but Fulham have opened talks with Bassey over a new contract and do not intend to sell him in January.

Thomas Frank has confirmed Crystal Palace are working to appoint Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, with a deal “very close.”

Frank was appointed the Eagles’ head coach this week, replacing the Frenchman Pierre Sage, who lasted just 16 matches in the job and left the club dead last in the Premier League.

As he looks to establish his coaching staff, though, Frank is looking into a reunion with Cueva. The pair were colleagues at Brentford between 2020 and 2024, when Cueva was poached by the Blues, who reportedly spent £1m to secure his services.

But Chelsea have upgraded on Cueva this season, signing Aston Villa’s Austin MacPhee in a similarly pricey move.

Palace have reportedly been in talks with Chelsea over Cueva’s transfer for some time, and Frank, speaking in his first press conference since taking over, has now confirmed the widespread reports that a deal is imminent.

Club Brugge winger Carlos Forbs is attracting a growing number of suiters, including Arsenal.

Fichajes reports that an impressive run of form in Belgium has alerted a number of Premier League clubs.

The 22-year-old has revitalised his career after difficult spells at Ajax and Wolves, producing five goals and eight assists in 15 appearances across all competitions this season.

Arsenal are continuing their search for a marquee forward ahead of the January transfer window.

Sky Sports report that the Premier League champions are tracking RB Leipzig’s Antonio Nusa and Brentford’s Kevin Schade as potential options, with a preference for a left-sided attacker capable of playing across the frontline.

Arsenal are also monitoring Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and could sell a midfielder to compete with Chelsea and Liverpool for the 23-year-old’s signature.

Manchester United have joined Tottenham in the race to sign Benfica striker Vangelis Pavlidis as Mauricio Pochettino looks to strengthen his attack in January.

The 27-year-old has scored 19 goals in 19 appearances across all competitions this season, attracting interest from several clubs.

CaughtOffside report that Pavlidis is open to a Premier League move, while United are also monitoring Victor Osimhen, Ivan Toney and Serhou Guirassy.

Pochettino is expected to receive backing in January as he looks to improve his squad, with defensive reinforcements also being considered.

Nico Paz is a transfer target for Manchester United following Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment as manager.

The Sun reports that Paz, who has sent a timely reminder of his talent after scoring two stunning goals for Argentina in their 7-0 victory over Costa Rica, is on United’s radar ahead of the January window.

Real Madrid retain an €80m option to re-sign Paz in 2027, while Arsenal, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain are also believed to be monitoring the Argentine.

Born in Tenerife, he began his career at Real Madrid before moving to Como in 2024.

Chelsea’s former techincal director Michael Emenalo has taken up an advisory role at Leicester City.

The Athletic reports that the Nigerian, who was with the Blues for five and a half years, is part of a team of consultants that is helping the Foxes with their future planning.

Manchester United are set to back Mauricio Pochettino the January transfer window.

Sky Sports reports that the Red Devils are prepared to sanction some signings for their new manager in the winter, with the club currently sat in the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino, who arrived at Carrington to begin work on Wednesday, will be tasked with guiding United away from the bottom three and as high up the top-flight table as he can, while also seeing how far he can get his new side in the Champions League.

Mauricio Pochettino has listed the three things he is hoping to bring to Manchester United in his first message to fans.

The Argentine arrived at his new club on Wednesday, touching down in Manchester immediately after overseeing his final game in charge of the United States.

In his first message to United fans, posted to the club’s social media channels, he said: “I am looking forward to meeting you guys.

“I have heard so many good things about you. I hope we bring all the happiness, working together and connect[ion], so that it is going to be a special season, and to make our players fight on the field and get the results we deserve.”

Manchester United have confirmed the departures of five members of staff after Mauricio Pochettino began work as the club’s new manager on Wednesday.

The Argentine was pictured arriving at Carrington for his first day in charge of the Red Devils, having flown immediately over after his final match with the United States.
